# Results — Study 48 (Groundhog): return seasonality on the S&P 500, 2000–2026

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Monthly returns of **398 current S&P 500
members** with ≥20y history (Yahoo). Each month, score every stock by its mean return in the *upcoming
calendar month* over the trailing 20 years; long the top quintile, short the bottom. As-of 2026-06;
inputs fingerprint `c768f59e31fe`.*

## The verdict, earned — Signal `REAL` · Tradability `FRAGILE` · "Genuinely same-month seasonal"? `CONFIRMED`

This is the rare one that **survives**. The claim sounds like numerology — a stock repeats its
calendar-month performance — yet the long-short earns **+7.3%/yr at a Sharpe of 0.81 (Lo t = 4.1)**,
wins 64% of months, and **does not decay** (Sharpe 0.81 both halves of the sample). And it is genuinely
*seasonal*: the control that ranks on *other* months' history earns **−3.3%/yr** — the predictability is
specific to the same calendar month, `CONFIRMED`. Tradability is `FRAGILE` rather than investable: the
break-even is a comfortable **38 bp/trade** and the net Sharpe is still **0.59 at 10 bp**, but the book
**reshuffles fully every month** (heavy turnover), needs **shorting ~80 names** (borrow costs and
hard-to-borrow frictions not in that 10 bp), and rests on a **survivorship-biased large-cap** panel. A
real, robust, *surprising* effect whose practical capture is the open question — not whether it exists.

## Data stamp

- **Universe**: 398 current S&P 500 members, ≥20y history, 2000-01 → 2026-06, 318 months, fingerprint
  `c768f59e31fe` (survivorship-biased, large-cap — stated)

## The effect is real — and specific to the same month

| | mean/yr | Sharpe | Lo t | hit rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **same-month seasonality** | **+7.3%** | **0.81** | **4.1** | 64% |
| control (other-month history) | −3.3% | −0.21 | −1.1 | 51% |

The same-month predictor pays strongly and significantly; ranking on *other* months' history does the
opposite. That contrast is the whole point — it rules out generic momentum and confirms a true calendar
seasonal (Heston & Sadka 2008). A t of 4.1 over 26 years is not a fluke.

## It hasn't decayed

| | same-month Sharpe |
|---|---|
| 1999–2012 | **0.81** |
| 2013–on | **0.81** |

Identical across halves — unusual for a published anomaly, and part of why the signal is `REAL`, not a
mined artifact.

## Why tradability is `FRAGILE`, not investable

| cost / trade | net Sharpe |
|---|---|
| gross | 0.81 |
| 5 bp | 0.70 |
| 10 bp | **0.59** |
| 20 bp | 0.38 |
| **break-even** | **≈ 38 bp** |

The edge clears realistic large-cap costs on paper — but three frictions the cost sweep doesn't capture
keep it `FRAGILE`: (1) the book turns over ~fully every month, (2) it requires a sizeable short book
(borrow fees, hard-to-borrow names), and (3) the universe is survivorship-biased large caps — the real
effect is strongest in smaller names, exactly where shorting and liquidity are worst. Real signal; the
net you can actually bank is uncertain.

## The honest takeaway

Return seasonality is the bench's outlier: a genuinely *strange* claim that **holds up** — significant
(t 4.1), same-month-specific (a clean control fails), and undecayed. `REAL` signal, `CONFIRMED`
seasonal. Whether you can *keep* it after monthly turnover, short-borrow and the small-cap frictions is
the live question — hence `FRAGILE`, not a free lunch. A reminder that the desk's job isn't to debunk
everything; sometimes the weird thing is true.
